arXiv:2602.08007v1 [cs.LG] 08 Feb 2026

From O⁡(m​n)O(mn) to O⁡(r2)O(r^{2}): Two-Sided Low-Rank Communication for Adam in Distributed Training with Memory Efficiency

Sizhe Dang ††thanks: equal contribution. Affiliation: Xi’an Jiaotong University Email: darknight1118@stu.xjtu.edu.cn    Jiaqi Shao11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Xi’an Jiaotong University Email: shaojiaqi@stu.xjtu.edu.cn    Xiaodong Zheng Affiliation: Xi’an Jiaotong University Email: zxd_xjtu@stu.xjtu.edu.cn    Guang Dai Affiliation: SGIT AI Lab Email: guang.dai@gmail.com    Yan Song Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China Email: clksong@gmail.com    Haishan Ye ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: Xi’an Jiaotong University Email: yehaishan@xjtu.edu.cn
Abstract

As foundation models continue to scale, pretraining increasingly relies on data-parallel distributed optimization, making bandwidth-limited gradient synchronization a key bottleneck. Orthogonally, projection-based low-rank optimizers were mainly designed for memory efficiency, but remain suboptimal for communication-limited training: one-sided synchronization still transmits an O⁡(r​n)O(rn) object for an m×nm\times n matrix gradient and refresh steps can dominate peak communicated bytes. We propose TSR, which brings two-sided low-rank communication to Adam-family updates (TSR-Adam) by synchronizing a compact core U⊤​G​V∈ℝr×rU^{\top}GV\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}, reducing the dominant per-step payload from O⁡(m​n)O(mn) to O⁡(r2)O(r^{2}) while keeping moment states in low-dimensional cores. To further reduce the peak communication from subspace refresh, TSR-Adam adopts a randomized SVD-based refresh that avoids full-gradient synchronization. We additionally extend low-rank communication to embedding gradients with embedding-specific ranks and refresh schedules, yielding additional communication and memory savings over keeping embeddings dense. Across pretraining from 60M to 1B model scales, TSR-Adam reduces average communicated bytes per step by 13×13\times, and on GLUE fine-tuning it reduces communication by 25×25\times, while achieving comparable performance; we further provide a theoretical stationarity analysis for the proposed update. Code is available at https://github.com/DKmiyan/TSR-Adam.

1 Introduction

Large-scale pretraining has established itself as the cornerstone of modern foundation models Brown et al. (2020); Bommasani (2021); Touvron et al. (2023). However, practical training at these scales relies heavily on distributed data-parallel execution, where synchronizing gradients across many accelerators can become a substantial bottleneck. This limitation is exacerbated by the disparity between high-bandwidth on-node interconnects and lower-bandwidth cross-node links (e.g., NVLink vs. PCIe), so communication overhead can quickly dominate once synchronization traverses bandwidth-limited boundaries. As model sizes and cluster scales grow, reducing the gradient synchronization volume becomes a central systems constraint for scalable pretraining Narayanan et al. (2021).

Existing work mitigates distributed-training overhead from multiple angles. System-level techniques such as sharding Rajbhandari et al. (2021) and generic compression Tang et al. (2021); Karimireddy et al. (2019) reduce the effective synchronization cost, but largely operate independently of the matrix representation being synchronized. Complementary to these system-level remedies, projection-based low-rank optimizers such as GaLore Zhao et al. (2024) maintain low-dimensional optimizer states for memory efficiency, yet remain suboptimal for communication-limited training: with one-sided projection, synchronizing an m×nm\times n matrix gradient still requires transmitting an O⁡(r​n)O(rn) (or O⁡(m​r)O(mr)) object, and SVD-style refresh can dominate the peak communicated bytes. Most recently, concurrent work such as GreedyLore Chen et al. (2025) augments GaLore-style low-rank compression with error feedback and improved guarantees; however, it inherits the GaLore-type one-sided communication object (scaling with a matrix dimension) and does not achieve the O⁡(r2)O(r^{2}) shared-core synchronization.

Motivated by a communication-first view of data-parallel training, we focus on the gradient as the synchronization object and measure efficiency by the transmitted bytes required to reach a target loss (Figure 1). For a matrix gradient G∈ℝm×nG\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, dense synchronization scales as O⁡(m​n)O(mn) per step, while one-sided low-rank methods still communicate an O⁡(r​n)O(rn) (or O⁡(m​r)O(mr)) factor and remain expensive when one dimension is large (Table 1). A natural way to break this scaling is to maintain two low-rank projection bases, U∈ℝm×rU\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r} and V∈ℝn×rV\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}, and synchronize only the core C=U⊤​G​V∈ℝr×rC=U^{\top}GV\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}, reducing the dominant payload to O⁡(r2)O(r^{2}) while storing Adam moments in the same core space. Making this approach practical hinges on two issues: (i) refresh steps must update base without falling back to full-gradient synchronization, otherwise peak communicated bytes can dominate; and (ii) communication-heavy layers should be accounted for explicitly, notably embeddings, which are often kept dense in prior low-rank treatments but can occupy a non-trivial fraction of synchronization volume (Figure 5).

To address these two issues, we propose TSR, a two-sided low-rank communication mechanism for data-parallel training; in this paper we instantiate TSR with Adam-family updates, yielding TSR-Adam(Figure 2). At each step, TSR-Adam synchronizes only the core C=U⊤​G​VC=U^{\top}GV and performs Adam moment updates in this same core space, reducing the dominant per-step communication from O⁡(m​n)O(mn) (dense) or O⁡(r​n)O(rn)/O⁡(m​r)O(mr) (one-sided) to O⁡(r2)O(r^{2}), while retaining low-dimensional moment states and thus the memory benefits of low-rank training. To ensure subspace maintenance does not dominate peak bytes, TSR-Adam refreshes the two projection bases via a randomized SVD procedure that communicates only low-dimensional sketches, avoiding full-gradient synchronization. We further apply the same low-rank communication principle to embedding gradients with embedding-specific ranks and refresh schedules, yielding additional communication and memory savings over keeping embeddings dense. We evaluate TSR-Adam on pretraining from 60M to 1B model scales and on GLUE fine-tuning benchmarks, and provide a convergence analysis for the resulting update. Overall, our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    Communication-first rethinking of low-rank optimizers. We demonstrate that projection-based low-rank optimizers, originally developed for memory efficiency, can be reframed as a communication mechanism. We optimize them explicitly for bandwidth-limited data-parallel training, surpassing the limitations of prior one-sided designs.

  • •

    Two-sided O⁡(r2)O(r^{2}) core synchronization with preserved memory benefits. We introduce TSR-Adam, which synchronizes a compact core C=U⊤​G​V∈ℝr×rC=U^{\top}GV\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r} for each matrix gradient, reducing the dominant per-step payload from O⁡(m​n)O(mn) (dense) and O⁡(r​n)O(rn) (one-sided) to O⁡(r2)O(r^{2}), while keeping Adam moment states in the same low-dimensional core space.

  • •

    Practical peak-byte reduction and embedding-aware design. We develop a randomized SVD-based refresh that avoids full-gradient synchronization to control peak communication on refresh steps, and we extend low-rank communication to embedding gradients with embedding-specific ranks and refresh schedules, yielding additional communication and memory savings over keeping embeddings dense.

  • •

    Empirical gains and theory. Across pretraining from 60M to 1B model scales, TSR-Adam reduces average communicated bytes per step by 13×13\times and on GLUE fine-tuning it reduces communication by 25×25\times, with comparable performance; we further provide a theoretical stationarity guarantee for the resulting update.

2 Related Work

Communication bottlenecks in large-scale LLM pretraining.

As foundation models continue to scale Brown et al. (2020); Bommasani (2021); Touvron et al. (2023), pretraining increasingly relies on data-parallel (often hybrid-parallel) distributed optimization, where dense gradient synchronization can become a dominant cost once training spans many devices and nodes Narayanan et al. (2021); Rasley et al. (2020); Shoeybi et al. (2019); Jiang et al. (2024). Prior work mitigates distributed training overheads through multiple routes: (i) state/gradient sharding such as ZeRO-style partitioning that removes redundancy across workers Rajbhandari et al. (2020); Rajbhandari et al. (2021); Zhao et al. (2023); (ii) quantization/compression that transmits low-bit updates with convergence guarantees (e.g., QSGD) Alistarh et al. (2017) and extends to adaptive optimizers (e.g., 1-bit Adam) Tang et al. (2021); (iii) sparsification that communicates only salient entries with error feedback/momentum correction (e.g., DGC) Lin et al. (2017); Karimireddy et al. (2019); and (iv) structured compression such as low-rank matrix-factor communication, where gradients are approximated by low-rank factors to reduce payload Vogels et al. (2019). Recent work also explores GaLore-style low-rank compression with improved error control and convergence analysis (e.g., GreedyLore) Chen et al. (2025). Importantly, most existing low-rank compressors synchronize factors or subspaces whose size still scales with at least one large matrix dimension (commonly O⁡(r⁡(m+n))O(r(m+n)) or O⁡(r​n)O(rn)), and subspace-refresh steps can induce pronounced peak communication.

Low-rank optimization for memory-efficient training.

In addition to bandwidth, LLM training is often constrained by memory due to optimizer states and activation storage. Low-rank methods reduce memory by restricting adaptation or optimization to compact subspaces. For parameter-efficient fine-tuning, LoRA Hu et al. (2022) injects trainable low-rank adapters while keeping pretrained weights frozen, with widely-used variants improving rank allocation, quantization, and stability (e.g., AdaLoRA, QLoRA, DoRA) Zhang et al. (2023); Dettmers et al. (2023); Liu et al. (2024). For pretraining and full-parameter learning, projection-based low-rank optimizers such as GaLore Zhao et al. (2024) maintain full-rank weights but project gradients into a learned low-rank subspace to reduce optimizer-state memory, with subsequent extensions improving scalability and refresh/staleness handling (e.g., GaLore 2, Tensor-GaLore; Online Subspace Descent; “Breaking the Frozen Subspace”) Su et al. (2025); George et al. (2024); Liang et al. (2024); Zhang et al. (2025). Overall, much of the low-rank optimizer literature is primarily driven by memory efficiency, whereas optimizing for communication-limited pretraining—especially achieving dimension-independent payload scaling and accounting for peak communicated bytes—remains comparatively under-explored.

3 Method

3.1 Background: AdamW

We consider data-parallel distributed training with NN workers. Let f⁡(w)f(w) denote the training objective and ww the model parameters. At step tt, worker ii computes a stochastic gradient gt,i=∇fi​(wt)g_{t,i}=\nabla f_{i}(w_{t}) over its local mini-batch. In standard data parallelism, the optimizer update is applied using the globally aggregated gradient

g¯t=1N​∑i=1Ngt,i,\bar{g}_{t}\;=\;\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}g_{t,i}, (1)

which is typically obtained via an all-reduce collective. For clarity, we first review the AdamW update under dense synchronization and then identify the tensors that must be communicated.

Dense AdamW update.

AdamW maintains first- and second-moment estimates (mt,vt)(m_{t},v_{t}) and applies decoupled weight decay. Given the aggregated gradient g¯t\bar{g}_{t}, the moment updates are

mt\displaystyle m_{t} =β1​mt−1+(1−β1)​g¯t,\displaystyle=\beta_{1}m_{t-1}+(1-\beta_{1})\,\bar{g}_{t}, (2)
vt\displaystyle v_{t} =β2​vt−1+(1−β2)​(g¯t∘g¯t),\displaystyle=\beta_{2}v_{t-1}+(1-\beta_{2})\,\big(\bar{g}_{t}\circ\bar{g}_{t}\big), (3)

followed by bias correction m^t=mt/(1−β1t)\hat{m}_{t}=m_{t}/(1-\beta_{1}^{t}) and v^t=vt/(1−β2t)\hat{v}_{t}=v_{t}/(1-\beta_{2}^{t}). The parameter update is

wt+1=wt−η⁡(m^tv^t+ϵ+λ​wt).w_{t+1}\;=\;w_{t}-\eta\left(\frac{\hat{m}_{t}}{\sqrt{\hat{v}_{t}}+\epsilon}+\lambda\,w_{t}\right). (4)

In distributed data parallelism, the communication-critical step is the construction of g¯t\bar{g}_{t} in (1); once g¯t\bar{g}_{t} is available, all remaining computations in (2)–(4) are local.

Matrix-shaped parameters.

Our method targets matrix-shaped parameter blocks, which constitute the dominant portion of trainable weights in transformers (e.g., linear and embedding matrices). For a matrix parameter block W(ℓ)∈ℝmℓ×nℓW^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{\ell}\times n_{\ell}}, let

Gt,i(ℓ):=∇W(ℓ)fi​(wt)∈ℝmℓ×nℓG_{t,i}^{(\ell)}\;:=\;\nabla_{W^{(\ell)}}f_{i}(w_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{\ell}\times n_{\ell}}

denote worker ii’s local gradient, and

G¯t(ℓ)=1N​∑i=1NGt,i(ℓ)\bar{G}_{t}^{(\ell)}\;=\;\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}G_{t,i}^{(\ell)}

the synchronized gradient used by dense AdamW. Dense synchronization communicates an mℓ×nℓm_{\ell}\times n_{\ell} tensor per step for each matrix block ℓ\ell, which scales with the full parameter size and can become the dominant bottleneck when interconnect bandwidth is limited.

3.2 Problem Formulation

We consider data-parallel training with NN workers and focus on matrix-shaped parameter blocks {W(ℓ)}ℓ∈ℒmat\{W^{(\ell)}\}_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}_{\text{mat}}}. At step tt, each worker ii computes a local matrix gradient Gt,i(ℓ)G_{t,i}^{(\ell)} and dense synchronization forms G¯t(ℓ)=1N​∑i=1NGt,i(ℓ)\bar{G}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}G_{t,i}^{(\ell)}, which is then used by AdamW. From a communication perspective, the key question is: what tensors must be synchronized across workers at each step?

For a given method, let 𝒮t(ℓ)\mathcal{S}_{t}^{(\ell)} denote the set of tensors synchronized for layer ℓ\ell at step tt. For dense AdamW, 𝒮t(ℓ)={G¯t(ℓ)}\mathcal{S}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\{\bar{G}_{t}^{(\ell)}\}. Low-rank communication replaces G¯t(ℓ)\bar{G}_{t}^{(\ell)} by compact representations, and may additionally synchronize auxiliary tensors on subspace-refresh steps.

Let bdtypeb_{\text{dtype}} be the number of bytes per element of the communicated dtype (e.g., 2 for bf16/fp16, 4 for fp32), and let |𝒮t(ℓ)||\mathcal{S}_{t}^{(\ell)}| denote the total number of scalar entries across all tensors in the set 𝒮t(ℓ)\mathcal{S}_{t}^{(\ell)}. We define the step-wise communicated bytes at step tt as

ℬt:=∑ℓ∈ℒmatbdtype⋅|𝒮t(ℓ)|.\mathcal{B}_{t}\;:=\;\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}_{\text{mat}}}b_{\text{dtype}}\cdot\big|\mathcal{S}_{t}^{(\ell)}\big|.

Over TT optimization steps, we further report the average communicated bytes per step, Bytes/Step:=1T​∑t=1Tℬt\mathrm{Bytes/Step}:=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathcal{B}_{t}, the peak communicated bytes per step, PeakBytes:=max1≤t≤T⁡ℬt\mathrm{PeakBytes}:=\max_{1\leq t\leq T}\mathcal{B}_{t}, and the cumulative communicated bytes up to step tt, CumulativeBytes⁡(t):=∑τ=1tℬτ\mathrm{CumulativeBytes}(t):=\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\mathcal{B}_{\tau}.

3.3 TSR-Adam: Two-Sided Low-Rank Core Synchronization

We compress and synchronize matrix gradients through a two-sided low-rank core representation. For each matrix-shaped parameter block W(ℓ)∈ℝmℓ×nℓW^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{\ell}\times n_{\ell}}, TSR-Adam maintains orthonormal bases Ut(ℓ)∈ℝmℓ×rℓU_{t}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{\ell}\times r_{\ell}} and Vt(ℓ)∈ℝnℓ×rℓV_{t}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\ell}\times r_{\ell}}, with (Ut(ℓ))⊤​Ut(ℓ)=I(U_{t}^{(\ell)})^{\top}U_{t}^{(\ell)}=I and (Vt(ℓ))⊤​Vt(ℓ)=I(V_{t}^{(\ell)})^{\top}V_{t}^{(\ell)}=I. At step tt, worker ii computes the local matrix gradient Gt,i(ℓ)G_{t,i}^{(\ell)} and forms the local core

Ct,i(ℓ):=(Ut(ℓ))⊤​Gt,i(ℓ)​Vt(ℓ)∈ℝrℓ×rℓ.C_{t,i}^{(\ell)}\;:=\;(U_{t}^{(\ell)})^{\top}G_{t,i}^{(\ell)}V_{t}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{r_{\ell}\times r_{\ell}}.

We then synchronize only the core via all-reduce, C¯t(ℓ)=1N​∑i=1NCt,i(ℓ)\bar{C}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}C_{t,i}^{(\ell)}, and reconstruct the gradient locally as

G^t(ℓ):=Ut(ℓ)​C¯t(ℓ)​(Vt(ℓ))⊤.\widehat{G}_{t}^{(\ell)}\;:=\;U_{t}^{(\ell)}\,\bar{C}_{t}^{(\ell)}\,(V_{t}^{(\ell)})^{\top}. (5)

Compared with dense synchronization of G¯t(ℓ)∈ℝmℓ×nℓ\bar{G}_{t}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{\ell}\times n_{\ell}}, this reduces the per-step synchronized payload for layer ℓ\ell from O⁡(mℓ​nℓ)O(m_{\ell}n_{\ell}) elements to O⁡(rℓ2)O(r_{\ell}^{2}) elements on non-refresh steps.

3.4 AdamW Updates in Core Space and Reconstruction

TSR-Adam performs AdamW updates using the synchronized two-sided core as the effective gradient. For each matrix block W(ℓ)W^{(\ell)}, we maintain AdamW first- and second-moment states mt(ℓ),vt(ℓ)∈ℝrℓ×rℓm_{t}^{(\ell)},v_{t}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{r_{\ell}\times r_{\ell}} in the low-dimensional core space. At step tt, after synchronizing the core C¯t(ℓ)=1N​∑i=1N(Ut(ℓ))⊤​Gt,i(ℓ)​Vt(ℓ)\bar{C}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(U_{t}^{(\ell)})^{\top}G_{t,i}^{(\ell)}V_{t}^{(\ell)}, we update

mt(ℓ)\displaystyle m_{t}^{(\ell)} =β1​mt−1(ℓ)+(1−β1)​C¯t(ℓ),\displaystyle=\beta_{1}m_{t-1}^{(\ell)}+(1-\beta_{1})\,\bar{C}_{t}^{(\ell)},
vt(ℓ)\displaystyle v_{t}^{(\ell)} =β2​vt−1(ℓ)+(1−β2)​(C¯t(ℓ)∘C¯t(ℓ)),\displaystyle=\beta_{2}v_{t-1}^{(\ell)}+(1-\beta_{2})\,\big(\bar{C}_{t}^{(\ell)}\circ\bar{C}_{t}^{(\ell)}\big),

where ∘\circ denotes the Hadamard (element-wise) product. With bias correction m^t(ℓ)=mt(ℓ)/(1−β1t)\hat{m}_{t}^{(\ell)}=m_{t}^{(\ell)}/(1-\beta_{1}^{t}) and v^t(ℓ)=vt(ℓ)/(1−β2t)\hat{v}_{t}^{(\ell)}=v_{t}^{(\ell)}/(1-\beta_{2}^{t}), the normalized update in core space is

Dt(ℓ)=m^t(ℓ)⊘(v^t(ℓ)+ϵ),D_{t}^{(\ell)}\;=\;\hat{m}_{t}^{(\ell)}\oslash\big(\sqrt{\hat{v}_{t}^{(\ell)}}+\epsilon\big),

where ⊘\oslash is element-wise division. We then lift the update back to the original parameter space via

Δ​Wt(ℓ)=Ut(ℓ)​Dt(ℓ)​(Vt(ℓ))⊤,\Delta W_{t}^{(\ell)}\;=\;U_{t}^{(\ell)}\,D_{t}^{(\ell)}\,(V_{t}^{(\ell)})^{\top},

and apply the standard AdamW rule

Wt+1(ℓ)=Wt(ℓ)−η⁡(Δ​Wt(ℓ)+λ​Wt(ℓ)).W_{t+1}^{(\ell)}\;=\;W_{t}^{(\ell)}-\eta\left(\Delta W_{t}^{(\ell)}+\lambda\,W_{t}^{(\ell)}\right).

All non-matrix parameters (e.g., biases and normalization parameters) are synchronized and updated in dense form.

3.5 Randomized Refresh of Two-Sided Bases and Peak Communication

The bases (Ut(ℓ),Vt(ℓ))(U_{t}^{(\ell)},V_{t}^{(\ell)}) must track the evolving gradient subspaces; stale bases can degrade the quality of the reconstructed update direction in Eq. (5).

A naive refresh strategy would first synchronize the full dense gradient G¯t(ℓ)\bar{G}_{t}^{(\ell)} and then compute an exact SVD, incurring both high compute cost and a large peak communication payload on refresh steps. Instead, we refresh (Ut(ℓ),Vt(ℓ))(U_{t}^{(\ell)},V_{t}^{(\ell)}) using a sketch-based randomized SVD (rSVD) procedure that avoids full-gradient synchronization and only requires communicating low-dimensional sketches.

Let kℓ=rℓ+pk_{\ell}=r_{\ell}+p with a small oversampling pp. On refresh steps (every KℓK_{\ell} steps), we draw a shared Gaussian matrix Ω(ℓ)∈ℝnℓ×kℓ\Omega^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\ell}\times k_{\ell}} (e.g., via RNG seed). Each worker ii forms a range sketch Yt,i(ℓ)=Gt,i(ℓ)​Ω(ℓ)Y_{t,i}^{(\ell)}=G_{t,i}^{(\ell)}\Omega^{(\ell)} then computes an orthonormal basis Qt,i(ℓ)=orth⁡(Yt,i(ℓ))Q_{t,i}^{(\ell)}=\mathrm{orth}(Y_{t,i}^{(\ell)}) (implemented by thin QR).

To improve the approximation when the spectrum decays slowly, we optionally apply qq steps of power iteration. In Algorithm 1 we show the case q=1q=1 for concreteness; larger qq follows by repeating the alternating multiplications. Concretely, for j=1,…,qj=1,\ldots,q, we compute

Yt,irow,(ℓ)=(Gt,i(ℓ))⊤​Qt,i(ℓ),Qt,irow,(ℓ)=orth⁡(Yt,irow,(ℓ)),\displaystyle{Y}_{t,i}^{\mathrm{row},(\ell)}\;=\;\!(G_{t,i}^{(\ell)})^{\top}Q_{t,i}^{(\ell)},\quad{Q}_{t,i}^{\mathrm{row},(\ell)}=\mathrm{orth}\!\left({Y}_{t,i}^{\mathrm{row},(\ell)}\right),
Yt,i(ℓ)=Gt,i(ℓ)​Qt,irow,(ℓ),Qt,i(ℓ)=orth⁡(Yt,i(ℓ)),\displaystyle{Y}_{t,i}^{(\ell)}\;=\;\!G_{t,i}^{(\ell)}{Q}_{t,i}^{\mathrm{row},(\ell)},\quad{Q}_{t,i}^{(\ell)}=\mathrm{orth}\!\left({Y}_{t,i}^{(\ell)}\right),

which matches the standard alternating multiplications by G(ℓ)G^{(\ell)} and (G(ℓ))⊤(G^{(\ell)})^{\top} in randomized SVD.

Given the final Qt,i(ℓ)Q_{t,i}^{(\ell)}, we form the reduced matrix

B¯t(ℓ):=(Qt(ℓ))⊤​G¯t(ℓ)=AR⁡((Qt,i(ℓ))⊤​Gt,i(ℓ)),\displaystyle\bar{B}_{t}^{(\ell)}\;:=\;(Q_{t}^{(\ell)})^{\top}\bar{G}_{t}^{(\ell)}\;=\;\operatorname{AR}\!\left((Q_{t,i}^{(\ell)})^{\top}G_{t,i}^{(\ell)}\right),
Q¯t(ℓ)=AR⁡(Qt,i(ℓ))\displaystyle\bar{Q}_{t}^{(\ell)}\;=\;\operatorname{AR}\!\left(Q_{t,i}^{(\ell)}\right)

and compute a small SVD B¯t(ℓ)=U~​Σ​V~⊤\bar{B}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\widetilde{U}\Sigma\widetilde{V}^{\top}. We then refresh the two-sided bases as

Ut(ℓ)←Q¯t(ℓ)U~[:,1:rℓ],Vt(ℓ)←V~[:,1:rℓ].U_{t}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\bar{Q}_{t}^{(\ell)}\,\widetilde{U}_{[:,1:r_{\ell}]},\qquad V_{t}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\widetilde{V}_{[:,1:r_{\ell}]}.

Accordingly, on non-refresh steps TSR-Adam synchronizes only 𝒮t(ℓ)={C¯t(ℓ)}\mathcal{S}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\{\bar{C}_{t}^{(\ell)}\}. On refresh steps, 𝒮t(ℓ)\mathcal{S}_{t}^{(\ell)} additionally includes the communicated sketches Q¯t(ℓ)\bar{Q}_{t}^{(\ell)} and B¯t(ℓ)\bar{B}_{t}^{(\ell)}, which determines the peak communicated bytes.

Importantly, refresh communicates only sketches of size mℓ​kℓm_{\ell}k_{\ell} or nℓ​kℓn_{\ell}k_{\ell} (repeated a small number of times when q>0q>0), rather than the full mℓ​nℓm_{\ell}n_{\ell} gradient, thereby substantially reducing the peak communicated bytes per step captured by PeakBytes\mathrm{PeakBytes}.

3.6 Embedding-Specific Low-Rank Communication

Embedding matrices can contribute a substantial fraction of communicated gradient volume, especially in smaller models. We therefore apply the same two-sided core synchronization to the embedding matrix E∈ℝ|𝒱|×dE\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|\times d}, but use a separate rank and refresh schedule, (remb,Kemb)(r_{\text{emb}},K_{\text{emb}}), from other linear layers. Concretely, we maintain Ut(emb)∈ℝ|𝒱|×rembU_{t}^{(\text{emb})}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|\times r_{\text{emb}}} and Vt(emb)∈ℝd×rembV_{t}^{(\text{emb})}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r_{\text{emb}}} and synchronize the embedding core Ct,i(emb)=(Ut(emb))⊤​Gt,i(emb)​Vt(emb)C_{t,i}^{(\text{emb})}=(U_{t}^{(\text{emb})})^{\top}G_{t,i}^{(\text{emb})}V_{t}^{(\text{emb})}. This decoupling allows TSR-Adam to tailor communication and refresh costs to the distinct structure of embeddings without constraining the choices for other matrix blocks.

3.7 Convergence Analysis

Providing convergence guarantees for fully adaptive Adam-family methods is notoriously delicate. Following the common practice in low-rank/subspace optimization (e.g., He et al. (2024); Zhang et al. (2025)), we therefore establish a stationarity guarantee for a momentum version of TSR that captures the core effect of two-sided projection and refresh; all proofs are deferred to Appendix B. Concretely, we analyze the update m~t:=Ut​mt​Vt⊤\widetilde{m}_{t}:=U_{t}m_{t}V_{t}^{\top} and wt+1=wt−η​m~tw_{t+1}=w_{t}-\eta\,\widetilde{m}_{t}.

Assumption (Smoothness).

The objective ff is LL-smooth, i.e., f⁡(y)≤f⁡(x)+⟨∇f​(x),y−x⟩+L2​‖y−x‖2f(y)\leq f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{L}{2}\|y-x\|^{2} for all x,yx,y.

Assumption (Projected Stochasticity and Approximation).

Let Pt:=UtUt⊤∇f(wt)VtVt⊤P_{t}:=U_{t}U_{t}^{\top}\nabla f(w_{t})V_{t}V_{t}^{\top} be the projection of the true gradient onto the current subspace. We define the subspace approximation error as Δt:=‖Pt−∇f​(wt)‖2\Delta_{t}:=\|P_{t}-\nabla f(w_{t})\|^{2}. Furthermore, we assume the synchronized core provides an unbiased estimate of the projected gradient, i.e., 𝔼⁡[Ut​C¯t​Vt⊤]=Pt\mathbb{E}[U_{t}\bar{C}_{t}V_{t}^{\top}]=P_{t}, with bounded variance 𝔼​‖Ut​C¯t​Vt⊤−Pt‖2≤σt2\mathbb{E}\|U_{t}\bar{C}_{t}V_{t}^{\top}-P_{t}\|^{2}\leq\sigma_{t}^{2}.

Theorem 1 (Stationarity bound).

Suppose the above assumptions hold. Set η=1L​T2/3\eta=\frac{1}{L\,T^{2/3}} and choose β2=1−40​L​η=1−40T1/3\beta^{2}=1-\sqrt{40L\eta}=1-\frac{\sqrt{40}}{T^{1/3}} (so 1−β2=40T1/31-\beta^{2}=\frac{\sqrt{40}}{T^{1/3}}). Define Δ​f:=𝔼⁡[f⁡(w0)−f⋆]\Delta f:=\mathbb{E}[f(w_{0})-f^{\star}], let 𝕀refresh​(t)∈{0,1}\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{refresh}}(t)\in\{0,1\} indicate whether step tt is a refresh step, and let Rt:=‖Ut​mt−1​Vt⊤−Ut−1​mt−1​Vt−1⊤‖2R_{t}:=\left\|U_{t}m_{t-1}V_{t}^{\top}\allowbreak-\allowbreak U_{t-1}m_{t-1}V_{t-1}^{\top}\right\|^{2}. Then for any T≥1T\geq 1,

1T​∑t=0T−1𝔼​‖∇f​(wt)‖2≤2​L​Δ​fT1/3+410​T2/3​𝔼​‖m~0−∇f​(w0)‖2+16T⋅40T1/3(1+1−40T1/3)2∑t=1T−1σt2+16T​(1+1−40T1/3)2∑t=1T−1Δt+(410​T2/3+85​T1/3)∑t=1T−1𝕀refresh(t)𝔼Rt.\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\|\nabla f(w_{t})\|^{2}\;\leq\;\frac{2L\,\Delta f}{T^{1/3}}+\frac{4}{\sqrt{10}\,T^{2/3}}\mathbb{E}\|\widetilde{m}_{0}-\nabla f(w_{0})\|^{2}+\\ \frac{16}{T}\cdot\frac{\frac{\sqrt{40}}{T^{1/3}}}{\Big(1+\sqrt{1-\frac{\sqrt{40}}{T^{1/3}}}\Big)^{2}}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\sigma_{t}^{2}+\frac{16}{T\Big(1+\sqrt{1-\frac{\sqrt{40}}{T^{1/3}}}\Big)^{2}}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\Delta_{t}\\ +\left(\frac{4}{\sqrt{10}\,T^{2/3}}+\frac{8}{5\,T^{1/3}}\right)\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{refresh}}(t)\,\mathbb{E}R_{t}. (6)
Remark 1 (Interpretation of Convergence Terms).

The bound effectively decomposes into three parts:

  • •

    Stochastic Error: Depends on the averaged projected variance σ¯2:=1T​∑tσt2\bar{\sigma}^{2}:=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t}\sigma_{t}^{2}, damped by a factor proportional to 1−β1-\beta, yielding an overall O~(T−1/3)⋅σ¯2\tilde{O}(T^{-1/3})\cdot\bar{\sigma}^{2} contribution.

  • •

    Approximation Floor: Scales with Δ¯:=1T​∑tΔt\bar{\Delta}:=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t}\Delta_{t}, forming an irreducible error floor. Notably, since gradients in large-scale training typically exhibit a low intrinsic dimension, Δ¯\bar{\Delta} remains naturally small, validating the effectiveness of our approach. However, if rank rr is chosen too small, Δ¯\bar{\Delta} will increase significantly, dominating the bound and leading to divergence.

  • •

    Refresh Trade-off: The refresh-mismatch term aggregates ∑𝕀refresh​(t)​𝔼​Rt\sum\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{refresh}}(t)\mathbb{E}R_{t}. This reflects a practical trade-off: larger KK reduces the number of refresh steps (lowering the sum count), whereas overly large KK may increase the subspace error Δt\Delta_{t} via staleness.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

We evaluate TSR on both pre-training and fine-tuning of LLMs. All experiments run on NVIDIA A100 GPUs and NVIDIA L40S GPUs.

Pre-training on C4. To evaluate its performance, we apply TSR to train LLaMA-based large language models Touvron et al. (2023) of four different scales—60M, 130M, 350M, and 1B—on the C4 dataset Raffel et al. (2020). The C4 dataset is a large, cleaned version of the Common Crawl web corpus, primarily designed for pre-training language models and learning word representations.

Fine-tuning on GLUE tasks. GLUE Wang et al. (2018) is a benchmark for evaluating the performance of NLP models on a variety of tasks, including sentiment analysis, question answering, and textual entailment. We use GLUE tasks to benchmark TSR against Adam and GaLore for communication efficient fine-tuning.

4.2 Main Results: Pretraining Communication Efficiency

TSR improves the loss–communication trade-off across model scales. Figure 4 and Table 3 show that TSR-Adam achieves pretraining loss comparable to dense AdamW and GaLore on 60M/130M/350M models. For LLaMA-1B, we report a representative run under limited training budget, and TSR still exhibits a highly competitive efficiency profile. Across all scales, TSR substantially reduces communication and peak traffic: compared to AdamW, it cuts Bytes/Step by up to 24×24\times, reduces PeakBytes by up to 59.72%, and lowers the memory footprint by up to 50%; averaged over scales, it achieves a 13×13\times reduction in Bytes/Step with consistent PeakBytes and memory savings. In addition, TSR’s per-step update time is lower than GaLore and remains comparable to dense AdamW.

TSR is more bytes-to-loss efficient under a fixed communication budget. On LLaMA-60M, we plot training loss against cumulative communicated bytes in Figure 1. TSR reaches comparable loss with markedly fewer communicated bytes, suggesting improved end-to-end communication efficiency beyond per-step compression. More results can be found in the Appendix C.

Embedding gradients are a non-trivial communication source, and compressing them matters. Embedding layers are often overlooked in low-rank optimization but can dominate communication in smaller models. Figure 5(a) shows that embeddings account for a significant fraction of gradient traffic. Applying TSR to embeddings with embedding-specific (remb,Kemb)(r_{\text{emb}},K_{\text{emb}}) further reduces total communication overhead while maintaining competitive pretraining loss (Figure 5(b)), supporting a holistic compression strategy that covers both linear and embedding matrices.

4.3 Ablations: Two-Sidedness, Randomized SVD, and Subspace Refresh Interval

We conduct ablation studies on the LLaMA-60M model to investigate the effects of two-sidedness, randomized SVD, and the subspace refresh interval on training convergence. The results are presented in Figure 3.

One-Side vs. Two-Side. The results indicate that the two-sided approach achieves comparable convergence to the one-sided variant while reducing the total communication volume by approximately two-thirds. This indicates that two-sided compression can substantially decrease communication costs at the expense of only a very small increase in final loss.

Normal SVD vs. Randomized SVD. The results indicate that using randomized SVD has little impact on convergence performance. Randomized SVD achieves a final loss comparable to that of standard SVD while using nearly half of the total communication volume. Moreover, our previous experiments indicate that, for models of the same scale, randomized SVD reduces the time required for subspace refreshes by approximately half.

Subspace Refresh Interval. The results indicate that a subspace refresh interval of 100 steps achieves the best convergence, while intervals of 50 or 200 steps incur degraded performance. Notably, excessively frequent refreshes, such as every 20 steps in our experiments, result in a pronounced increase in communication overhead.

4.4 Fine-tuning Results

We fine-tuned pre-trained RoBERTa-Base Liu et al. (2019) model on the GLUE tasks, and the results are shown in Table 4. Our method achieves better or comparable performance to GaLore on 6 of the 8 tasks, while requiring only one-eighth of the bytes per step. Compared to Adam, our method reduces the bytes per step by approximately 25×, while incurring only a 0.86% drop in average task performance. See the Appendix C for parameter settings and convergence graphs for each dataset.

5 Conclusion

We propose TSR, a two-sided low-rank communication mechanism for distributed training of large language models. By synchronizing only a compact core U⊤​G​V∈ℝr×rU^{\top}GV\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}, TSR reduces the dominant per-step communication from dense O⁡(m​n)O(mn) to O⁡(r2)O(r^{2}), while keeping optimizer states in the same low-dimensional core space. To control refresh-induced peak traffic, TSR adopts a randomized SVD-based refresh that communicates only low-dimensional sketches. We further extend the same principle to embedding gradients via embedding-specific ranks and refresh schedules. Empirically, TSR substantially improves bytes-to-loss efficiency in pretraining and fine-tuning.

Appendix A Related Works

Communication Bottlenecks in Large-Scale Pretraining of LLMs

The training of large language models at scale is often limited not by compute, but by communication overhead. When hundreds or thousands of GPUs are used in distributed data-parallel training, the cost of synchronizing gradients and model updates over interconnects (PCIe, NVLink, InfiniBand/Ethernet) can dominate the iteration time Tang et al. [2021], Narayanan et al. [2021]. In modern LLM pretraining runs, network bandwidth becomes a primary bottleneck – for example, multi-node training must send enormous gradients (on the order of billions of parameters) across relatively slower inter-node links, leading to idle compute while GPUs wait on data exchange Narayanan et al. [2021]. This has motivated a long line of communication-efficient optimization techniques to alleviate bandwidth limitations in distributed training of foundation models.

Optimizer state sharding. One approach is to eliminate redundant data transfers by partitioning or sharding optimizer states across workers. ZeRO (Zero Redundancy Optimizer) introduced by Rajbhandari et al Rajbhandari et al. [2020]. shards the gradient histories and optimizer momentum/variance so that each GPU only stores (and communicates) a fraction of the full state, instead of replicating it on all GPUs. By stripping away duplicate communication and memory, ZeRO achieved near-linear scaling for models up to 100+ billion parameters, retaining low communication volume despite massive model size Rajbhandari et al. [2020]. This idea underpins Fully Sharded Data Parallel schemes, ensuring that bandwidth usage grows sub-linearly with the number of accelerators.

Gradient quantization and compression. Another class of methods reduces the number of bits or values that need to be exchanged each step. For instance, QSGD (Alistarh et al., 2017) proposed quantizing gradients to low-bit representations, showing one can trade off communication bandwidth for convergence time by sending fewer bits per gradient component Alistarh et al. [2017]. Such lossy compression directly targets the “high bandwidth cost of communicating gradient updates” in parallel SGD Alistarh et al. [2017]. Following this, researchers developed 1-bit SGD/Adam techniques that transmit only a 1-bit sign or compressed form of each gradient with error compensation. Notably, 1-bit Adam Tang et al. [2021]demonstrated up to 5× reduction in communication volume with no loss in convergence speed compared to uncompressed Adam. This was achieved by accumulating quantization errors and leveraging the stability of Adam’s second moment estimates. Similarly, techniques for 8-bit compression of gradients/updates have been explored – for example, Dettmers et al. developed 8-bit optimizers that store and communicate optimizer statistics at 8-bit precision while preserving 32-bit performance Dettmers et al. [2021]. By quantizing gradient exchanges (e.g. 8-bit or even 4-bit), these methods cut bandwidth requirements substantially, at the cost of minimal noise that can be mitigated with proper tuning.

Gradient sparsification. In parallel, researchers have investigated sending only a subset of gradient elements to reduce traffic. Deep Gradient Compression (DGC) Lin et al. [2017] showed that 99.9% of gradient values in distributed training can be deemed redundant and pruned away with little impact on model quality. DGC aggressively sparsifies gradients (e.g. by transmitting only the top-kk magnitude components) and uses techniques like momentum correction and warm-up to preserve accuracy Lin et al. [2017]. The result was a 270×–600× compression of gradient data (e.g. reducing a ResNet-50 gradient from 97 MB to 0.35 MB) without loss of accuracy Lin et al. [2017]. Such extreme compression allowed training on bandwidth-limited 1 Gbps Ethernet clusters that would otherwise be prohibitively slow Lin et al. [2017]. Gradient sparsification and pruning, combined with error-feedback mechanisms, continue to be effective for cutting down communication in large-scale setups.

Low-rank gradient communication. More recently, structured approaches have been proposed to compress gradients by exploiting linear correlations. PowerSGD Vogels et al. [2019] is a representative method that approximates the gradient matrix in each layer by a low-rank factorization and only communicates the low-rank factors. By using a small rank (e.g. r=1r=1 or 44) and a power iteration method to find these factors, PowerSGD can drastically reduce bandwidth while maintaining final accuracy close to full-precision SGD. It was one of the first schemes to demonstrate actual wall-clock speedups in distributed training owing to communication savings Vogels et al. [2019]. Related work has combined low-rank compression with second-order information – for example, using a natural gradient low-rank scheme that preconditions updates. Mu et al. (2023) showed that a hybrid low-rank natural gradient method can reduce communication time by over an order of magnitude (up to 10.7×10.7\times) on multi-GPU training, thanks to smaller transmitted updates and fewer synchronization steps Mu et al. [2022]. Overall, by compressing gradients via quantization, sparsity, or low-rank approximation, distributed LLM training can significantly mitigate network bottlenecks and push closer to the limits of hardware bandwidth. These communication-efficient optimizers have become crucial as model sizes and cluster scales continue to grow, ensuring that networking infrastructure does not become the rate limiter in large-scale pretraining.

Low-Rank Optimization for Memory-Efficient Training

Scaling up model size not only stresses communication, but also introduces severe memory and compute challenges. Modern LLMs with billions of parameters demand enormous memory to store model weights, optimizer states, and gradients. For example, training a 7B-parameter transformer from scratch with Adam optimizer can require on the order of 60 GB of memory per GPU, with optimizer momentum and variance states taking much more space than the weights themselves Zhao et al. [2024]. To address this, researchers have explored low-rank optimization methods that reduce memory and compute usage by restricting updates to low-dimensional subspaces.

Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). A classical approach for memory-efficient training is to constrain weight updates to a low-rank form. LoRA Hu et al. [2022] injects trainable low-rank matrices into each layer’s weights instead of updating the full weight matrix Zhao et al. [2024]. In LoRA, a pre-trained weight W0W_{0} is frozen and two small rank-rr matrices U,VU,V are learned such that W=W0+U​VTW=W_{0}+UV^{T}. Because UU and VV have far fewer parameters than WW (with r≪dim​(W)r\ll\text{dim}(W)), the number of trainable parameters – and crucially the optimizer states for them – are dramatically reduced Zhao et al. [2024]. LoRA proved to be an efficient fine-tuning strategy, cutting memory usage while maintaining decent performance on downstream tasks. However, LoRA’s low-rank constraint can become a limitation in full training: the model is confined to a tiny subspace of the full parameter space. Recent studies found that LoRA fine-tuning often cannot match the accuracy of full-model tuning, and in pre-training from scratch it may even require a full-rank warm-up phase before low-rank updates are viable Zhao et al. [2024]. In essence, if the true optimal weights are not low-rank or if the low-rank reparameterization alters training dynamics, a fixed small subspace can hurt convergence. This motivates methods that preserve the flexibility of full-rank training while still reaping memory savings from low-rank structures.

Gradient low-rank projection (GaLore). Instead of freezing weights to a low-rank form, one can project gradients onto a low-rank subspace during training. GaLore Zhao et al. [2024] is an optimizer that maintains full-rank model weights but restricts each weight’s gradient to a learned low-rank subspace. The key insight is that as training progresses, the gradients of large models often lie in a much lower-dimensional subspace than the parameter count – they have a slowly changing, low-rank structure. GaLore periodically computes a small set of basis vectors (e.g. via SVD on recent gradients) and projects incoming gradients onto this subspace, then applies the optimizer (Adam, Adagrad, etc.) in the compressed space Zhao et al. [2024]. By doing so, the memory-heavy optimizer states (momentum, etc.) are only kept for the low-rank coordinates rather than for every parameter. This approach allows full-parameter training (no accuracy drop from restricting model capacity) but yields major memory savings: GaLore reports up to a 65% reduction in optimizer memory compared to standard Adam, and up to 82% reduction when combined with 8-bit quantized states Zhao et al. [2024]. In practice, GaLore enabled, for the first time, pre-training a 7B LLM on a single 24 GB GPU without any offloading or model-parallel tricks Zhao et al. [2024]. Compared to LoRA, which limits the model to a fixed low-rank, GaLore’s online subspace descent allows the subspace to evolve – e.g. updating the projection basis every few hundred steps – which was shown to preserve model quality while still reducing memory by 3̃0% relative to LoRA’s approach.

Extensions of GaLore. The idea of low-rank optimizer updates has spurred many follow-ups. Some works add quantization and other structure on top of GaLore – for example, 8-bit GaLore quantizes the projected gradients to further cut memory, and researchers have explored using higher-order tensor decompositions (Tensor-GaLore George et al. [2024]) to compress gradients along multiple modes Su et al. [2025]. These improvements address practical bottlenecks: GaLore’s original implementation incurred non-negligible SVD computation for subspace updates and didn’t natively support sharded data parallel. In GaLore 2 Su et al. [2025], the framework was optimized with fast randomized SVD updates and integration into PyTorch’s Fully Sharded Data Parallel, making it efficient and scalable for real-world runs. GaLore 2 demonstrated the ability to pre-train a LLaMA-7B model on 500 billion tokens using low-rank gradient projection, indicating that such methods can indeed support large-scale training without hitting memory limits. Beyond GaLore itself, researchers have looked at the connection between gradient subspaces and weight matrices. JAISWAL et al. [2025] observed that as training converges, certain layers’ gradients stabilize in a low-rank subspace and correspondingly the weights exhibit implicit low-rank structure. They introduced WeLore (Weight Low-Rank Projection), a one-shot compression technique that leverages these observations: after pretraining, it categorizes weight matrices into those that can be compressed (low-rank) and those that cannot, and compresses the former for memory-efficient fine-tuning or inference JAISWAL et al. [2025]. WeLore essentially unifies model compression with the low-rank training insights from GaLore, achieving significant memory reduction with minimal performance drop by tailoring the rank per layer.

Dynamic subspace and theoretical advances. An important question for low-rank training is how to choose and update the subspace. If the subspace is too restrictive or is not refreshed, training can stagnate. Zhang et al. [2025] highlighted this in “Breaking the Frozen Subspace”: they found that methods like GaLore which pick the dominant gradient subspace can suffer because the top principal components of the gradient stop changing over time, effectively freezing the update directions. To counter this, they proposed an importance sampling strategy that occasionally forces exploration of new random directions outside the current subspace, and proved that this yields convergence guarantees that the purely dominant subspace approach lacks. Empirically, their method outperformed prior low-rank optimizers in LLM pretraining, underlining the need to keep the optimization subspace from becoming too static. On the theoretical side, He et al. [2024] examined GaLore’s convergence properties and showed that GaLore may fail to converge in stochastic training unless certain conditions (large batch sizes or isotropic gradient noise) hold. They introduced a variant called GoLore (Gradient random Low-Rank projection) that uses randomization in the projection step, and proved it converges reliably in standard SGD settings. This work provides formal guarantees for subspace optimization algorithms and guides how to design low-rank updates that are stable in theory as well as practice.

Finally, researchers have begun integrating low-rank methods with second-order optimization and manifold geometry. Natural GaLore Das [2024] is one such approach that applies a Riemannian preconditioning to GaLore’s low-rank updates. By multiplying the low-rank gradient by the inverse Fisher information matrix (estimated efficiently via the Woodbury identity), Natural GaLore accelerates convergence without additional memory overhead. This can be seen as performing natural gradient descent within the low-rank subspace, yielding faster loss reduction especially when the training budget (number of steps) is limited. In a similar vein, Mo et al. [2025]proposed LORO (Low-Rank Riemannian Optimizer) for full low-rank pretraining. Instead of maintaining a full-rank model, LORO parameterizes each weight matrix as the product of two rank-rr factors from scratch and optimizes these factors jointly on the appropriate Riemannian manifold. By updating the factor pair in tandem along the manifold’s steepest descent direction (avoiding any reconstruction of full-sized gradients), LORO manages to learn low-rank models that match or even exceed the quality of full models, while using far less memory. Notably, an LLM pre-trained with LORO (rank 256 on a 1B parameter model) reached a slightly better perplexity than a full model, despite using  54% less memory and achieving 1.8× faster training and 2.2× faster inference throughput. Such results are encouraging as they suggest that, with proper optimization on the low-rank manifold, we can attain the dual goals of memory efficiency and high performance. In summary, a rich landscape of low-rank optimization methods – from practical GaLore-based techniques to theoretical and second-order enhancements – has emerged to enable memory-efficient training of large models. These works collectively pave the way for optimizers that address both communication and memory bottlenecks in large-scale LLM pretraining, which is precisely the gap our proposed method aims to fill.

B.3 Part 3: Refresh steps and a unified recursion with an RtR_{t} term

In this part we incorporate the effect of refreshing Ut,VtU_{t},V_{t} (i.e., Ut≠Ut−1U_{t}\neq U_{t-1} and/or Vt≠Vt−1V_{t}\neq V_{t-1}), and derive a unified one-step recursion that holds for both refresh and non-refresh steps.

Notation.

Define the tracking error

Et:=𝔼​‖Ut​mt​Vt⊤−∇f​(wt)‖2.E_{t}\;:=\;\mathbb{E}\left\|U_{t}m_{t}V_{t}^{\top}-\nabla f(w_{t})\right\|^{2}. (41)

Let 𝕀refresh\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{refresh}} be the indicator of a refresh step, i.e., 𝕀refresh=1\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{refresh}}=1 if tmodK=0t\bmod K=0 and 𝕀refresh=0\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{refresh}}=0 otherwise.

Step 1: A bound for the wt−1w_{t-1} tracking term under refresh.

At a refresh step, we need to relate ‖Ut​mt−1​Vt⊤−∇f​(wt−1)‖2\left\|U_{t}m_{t-1}V_{t}^{\top}-\nabla f(w_{t-1})\right\|^{2} to the previous-basis quantity ‖Ut−1​mt−1​Vt−1⊤−∇f​(wt−1)‖2\left\|U_{t-1}m_{t-1}V_{t-1}^{\top}-\nabla f(w_{t-1})\right\|^{2}.

Write

Ut​mt−1​Vt⊤−∇f​(wt−1)\displaystyle U_{t}m_{t-1}V_{t}^{\top}-\nabla f(w_{t-1}) =(Ut​mt−1​Vt⊤−Ut−1​mt−1​Vt−1⊤)⏟=:Atref+(Ut−1​mt−1​Vt−1⊤−∇f​(wt−1))⏟=:Bt−1.\displaystyle=\underbrace{\Big(U_{t}m_{t-1}V_{t}^{\top}-U_{t-1}m_{t-1}V_{t-1}^{\top}\Big)}_{=:A_{t}^{\mathrm{ref}}}+\underbrace{\Big(U_{t-1}m_{t-1}V_{t-1}^{\top}-\nabla f(w_{t-1})\Big)}_{=:B_{t-1}}. (42)

Using the splitting inequality (Young), for any γ>0\gamma>0,

‖Atref+Bt−1‖2≤(1+1γ)​‖Atref‖2+(1+γ)​‖Bt−1‖2.\|A_{t}^{\mathrm{ref}}+B_{t-1}\|^{2}\leq\left(1+\frac{1}{\gamma}\right)\|A_{t}^{\mathrm{ref}}\|^{2}+(1+\gamma)\|B_{t-1}\|^{2}. (43)

Choose

γ:=1−β28,\gamma:=\frac{1-\beta^{2}}{8}, (44)

so that

1+γ=1+1−β28,1+1γ=1+81−β2.1+\gamma=1+\frac{1-\beta^{2}}{8},\qquad 1+\frac{1}{\gamma}=1+\frac{8}{1-\beta^{2}}. (45)

Then (42)–(45) imply

‖Ut​mt−1​Vt⊤−∇f​(wt−1)‖2≤\displaystyle\left\|U_{t}m_{t-1}V_{t}^{\top}-\nabla f(w_{t-1})\right\|^{2}\leq\; (1+81−β2)​‖Ut​mt−1​Vt⊤−Ut−1​mt−1​Vt−1⊤‖2\displaystyle\left(1+\frac{8}{1-\beta^{2}}\right)\left\|U_{t}m_{t-1}V_{t}^{\top}-U_{t-1}m_{t-1}V_{t-1}^{\top}\right\|^{2}
+(1+1−β28)​‖Ut−1​mt−1​Vt−1⊤−∇f​(wt−1)‖2.\displaystyle+\left(1+\frac{1-\beta^{2}}{8}\right)\left\|U_{t-1}m_{t-1}V_{t-1}^{\top}-\nabla f(w_{t-1})\right\|^{2}. (46)

Step 2: Plug the refresh bound into the no-refresh recursion from Part 2.

From Part 2, we already have (for any step tt) the inequality

Et≤\displaystyle E_{t}\leq\; (1−1−β24)​𝔼​‖Ut​mt−1​Vt⊤−∇f​(wt−1)‖2+5−β21−β2​L2​𝔼​‖wt−wt−1‖2\displaystyle\left(1-\frac{1-\beta^{2}}{4}\right)\,\mathbb{E}\left\|U_{t}m_{t-1}V_{t}^{\top}-\nabla f(w_{t-1})\right\|^{2}+\frac{5-\beta^{2}}{1-\beta^{2}}\,L^{2}\,\mathbb{E}\|w_{t}-w_{t-1}\|^{2}
+2​(1−β)2​σt2+2​(1−β)1+β​Δt.\displaystyle+2(1-\beta)^{2}\sigma_{t}^{2}+\frac{2(1-\beta)}{1+\beta}\Delta_{t}. (47)

If tt is a refresh step, apply (46) inside (47):

Et≤\displaystyle E_{t}\leq\; (1−1−β24)​(1+1−β28)​𝔼​‖Ut−1​mt−1​Vt−1⊤−∇f​(wt−1)‖2\displaystyle\left(1-\frac{1-\beta^{2}}{4}\right)\left(1+\frac{1-\beta^{2}}{8}\right)\mathbb{E}\left\|U_{t-1}m_{t-1}V_{t-1}^{\top}-\nabla f(w_{t-1})\right\|^{2}
+(1−1−β24)​(1+81−β2)​𝔼​‖Ut​mt−1​Vt⊤−Ut−1​mt−1​Vt−1⊤‖2\displaystyle+\left(1-\frac{1-\beta^{2}}{4}\right)\left(1+\frac{8}{1-\beta^{2}}\right)\mathbb{E}\left\|U_{t}m_{t-1}V_{t}^{\top}-U_{t-1}m_{t-1}V_{t-1}^{\top}\right\|^{2}
+5−β21−β2​L2​𝔼​‖wt−wt−1‖2+2​(1−β)2​σt2+2​(1−β)1+β​Δt.\displaystyle+\frac{5-\beta^{2}}{1-\beta^{2}}\,L^{2}\,\mathbb{E}\|w_{t}-w_{t-1}\|^{2}+2(1-\beta)^{2}\sigma_{t}^{2}+\frac{2(1-\beta)}{1+\beta}\Delta_{t}. (48)

Now we simplify the coefficients without skipping steps. Let x:=1−β2∈(0,1]x:=1-\beta^{2}\in(0,1]. Then

(1−x4)​(1+x8)\displaystyle\left(1-\frac{x}{4}\right)\left(1+\frac{x}{8}\right) =1+x8−x4−x232=1−x8−x232≤1−x8=1−1−β28.\displaystyle=1+\frac{x}{8}-\frac{x}{4}-\frac{x^{2}}{32}=1-\frac{x}{8}-\frac{x^{2}}{32}\leq 1-\frac{x}{8}=1-\frac{1-\beta^{2}}{8}. (49)

Applying (49) and (50) to (48), we get

Et≤\displaystyle E_{t}\leq\; (1−1−β28)​𝔼​‖Ut−1​mt−1​Vt−1⊤−∇f​(wt−1)‖2+α​Rt\displaystyle\left(1-\frac{1-\beta^{2}}{8}\right)\mathbb{E}\left\|U_{t-1}m_{t-1}V_{t-1}^{\top}-\nabla f(w_{t-1})\right\|^{2}+\alpha R_{t}
+5−β21−β2​L2​𝔼​‖wt−wt−1‖2+2​(1−β)2​σt2+2​(1−β)1+β​Δt,\displaystyle+\frac{5-\beta^{2}}{1-\beta^{2}}\,L^{2}\,\mathbb{E}\|w_{t}-w_{t-1}\|^{2}+2(1-\beta)^{2}\sigma_{t}^{2}+\frac{2(1-\beta)}{1+\beta}\Delta_{t}, (51)

where we define the refresh mismatch term (kept for later analysis) as

Rt:=𝔼​‖Ut​mt−1​Vt⊤−Ut−1​mt−1​Vt−1⊤‖2.R_{t}:=\mathbb{E}\left\|U_{t}m_{t-1}V_{t}^{\top}-U_{t-1}m_{t-1}V_{t-1}^{\top}\right\|^{2}. (52)
α:=1+81−β2.\alpha~:=~1+\frac{8}{1-\beta^{2}}. (53)

Step 3: A unified recursion for all steps.

If tt is not a refresh step, then Ut=Ut−1U_{t}=U_{t-1} and Vt=Vt−1V_{t}=V_{t-1}, hence

‖Ut​mt−1​Vt⊤−Ut−1​mt−1​Vt−1⊤‖2=0,\left\|U_{t}m_{t-1}V_{t}^{\top}-U_{t-1}m_{t-1}V_{t-1}^{\top}\right\|^{2}=0, (54)

and from (47) we also have the stronger contraction (1−1−β24)≤(1−1−β28)\left(1-\frac{1-\beta^{2}}{4}\right)\leq\left(1-\frac{1-\beta^{2}}{8}\right). Therefore, combining both cases yields the unified bound

Et≤\displaystyle E_{t}\leq\; (1−1−β28)​𝔼​‖Ut−1​mt−1​Vt−1⊤−∇f​(wt−1)‖2+α​𝕀refresh⋅Rt\displaystyle\left(1-\frac{1-\beta^{2}}{8}\right)\mathbb{E}\left\|U_{t-1}m_{t-1}V_{t-1}^{\top}-\nabla f(w_{t-1})\right\|^{2}+\alpha\,\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{refresh}}\cdot R_{t}
+5−β21−β2​L2​𝔼​‖wt−wt−1‖2+2​(1−β)2​σt2+2​(1−β)1+β​Δt.\displaystyle+\frac{5-\beta^{2}}{1-\beta^{2}}\,L^{2}\,\mathbb{E}\|w_{t}-w_{t-1}\|^{2}+2(1-\beta)^{2}\sigma_{t}^{2}+\frac{2(1-\beta)}{1+\beta}\Delta_{t}. (55)

We will keep the term 𝕀refresh⋅Rt\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{refresh}}\cdot R_{t} as is for now and discuss how to further control it later.

B.4 Part 4: Summing the recursion via a geometric-series lemma

We start from the unified one-step recursion in (55):

Et≤\displaystyle E_{t}\leq\; (1−ρ)​Et−1+α​𝕀refresh⋅Rt+A​L2​𝔼​‖wt−wt−1‖2+B​σt2+C​Δt,\displaystyle\left(1-\rho\right)E_{t-1}+\alpha\,\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{refresh}}\cdot R_{t}+A\,L^{2}\,\mathbb{E}\|w_{t}-w_{t-1}\|^{2}+B\,\sigma_{t}^{2}+C\,\Delta_{t}, (56)

where we denote

ρ:=1−β28,A:=5−β21−β2,B:=2​(1−β)2,C:=2​(1−β)1+β,\rho:=\frac{1-\beta^{2}}{8},\qquad A:=\frac{5-\beta^{2}}{1-\beta^{2}},\qquad B:=2(1-\beta)^{2},\qquad C:=\frac{2(1-\beta)}{1+\beta}, (57)

and Et:=𝔼​‖Ut​mt​Vt⊤−∇f​(wt)‖2E_{t}:=\mathbb{E}\|U_{t}m_{t}V_{t}^{\top}-\nabla f(w_{t})\|^{2}.

Lemma 1 (Summation of a linear contraction recursion).

Let {at}t≥0\{a_{t}\}_{t\geq 0} be a nonnegative sequence satisfying, for some ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1),

at≤(1−ρ)​at−1+bt,∀t≥1,a_{t}\leq(1-\rho)a_{t-1}+b_{t},\qquad\forall t\geq 1, (58)

where bt≥0b_{t}\geq 0 for all tt. Then for any integer T≥1T\geq 1,

∑t=0T−1at≤1ρ​a0+1ρ​∑t=1T−1bt.\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}a_{t}\leq\frac{1}{\rho}\,a_{0}+\frac{1}{\rho}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}b_{t}. (59)
Proof.

Unrolling (58) yields, for t≥1t\geq 1,

at≤(1−ρ)t​a0+∑k=1t(1−ρ)t−k​bk.a_{t}\leq(1-\rho)^{t}a_{0}+\sum_{k=1}^{t}(1-\rho)^{t-k}b_{k}. (60)

Summing (60) over t=1,…,T−1t=1,\dots,T-1 and adding a0a_{0} gives

∑t=0T−1at\displaystyle\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}a_{t} ≤a0+a0​∑t=1T−1(1−ρ)t+∑t=1T−1∑k=1t(1−ρ)t−k​bk\displaystyle\leq a_{0}+a_{0}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}(1-\rho)^{t}+\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\sum_{k=1}^{t}(1-\rho)^{t-k}b_{k}
≤a0​∑t=0∞(1−ρ)t+∑k=1T−1bk​∑j=0∞(1−ρ)j\displaystyle\leq a_{0}\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}(1-\rho)^{t}+\sum_{k=1}^{T-1}b_{k}\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}(1-\rho)^{j}
=1ρ​a0+1ρ​∑k=1T−1bk,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\rho}a_{0}+\frac{1}{\rho}\sum_{k=1}^{T-1}b_{k}, (61)

which proves (59). ∎

Apply Lemma 1 to (56).

We match Lemma 1 by setting

at:=Et,bt:=α𝕀refresh⋅Rt+AL2𝔼∥wt−wt−1∥2+Bσt2+CΔt,(t≥1),a_{t}:=E_{t},\qquad b_{t}:=\alpha\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{refresh}}\cdot R_{t}+A\,L^{2}\,\mathbb{E}\|w_{t}-w_{t-1}\|^{2}+B\,\sigma_{t}^{2}+C\,\Delta_{t},\qquad(t\geq 1), (62)

and ρ=1−β28\rho=\frac{1-\beta^{2}}{8} as in (57). Since all terms on the right-hand side are nonnegative, the conditions of Lemma 1 hold.

Therefore, for any T≥1T\geq 1,

∑t=0T−1Et≤\displaystyle\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}E_{t}\leq\; 1ρ​E0+1ρ​∑t=1T−1(α​𝕀refresh⋅Rt+A​L2​𝔼​‖wt−wt−1‖2+B​σt2+C​Δt).\displaystyle\frac{1}{\rho}E_{0}+\frac{1}{\rho}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\left(\alpha\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{refresh}}\cdot R_{t}+A\,L^{2}\,\mathbb{E}\|w_{t}-w_{t-1}\|^{2}+B\,\sigma_{t}^{2}+C\,\Delta_{t}\right). (63)

Simplify the coefficients (explicitly).

Using ρ=1−β28\rho=\frac{1-\beta^{2}}{8}, we have 1ρ=81−β2\frac{1}{\rho}=\frac{8}{1-\beta^{2}}. Then each term in (63) becomes:

1ρ⋅A\displaystyle\frac{1}{\rho}\cdot A =81−β2⋅5−β21−β2=8​(5−β2)(1−β2)2,\displaystyle=\frac{8}{1-\beta^{2}}\cdot\frac{5-\beta^{2}}{1-\beta^{2}}=\frac{8(5-\beta^{2})}{(1-\beta^{2})^{2}}, (64)
1ρ⋅B\displaystyle\frac{1}{\rho}\cdot B =81−β2⋅2​(1−β)2=16​(1−β)2(1−β)​(1+β)=16​(1−β)1+β,\displaystyle=\frac{8}{1-\beta^{2}}\cdot 2(1-\beta)^{2}=\frac{16(1-\beta)^{2}}{(1-\beta)(1+\beta)}=\frac{16(1-\beta)}{1+\beta}, (65)
1ρ⋅C\displaystyle\frac{1}{\rho}\cdot C =81−β2⋅2​(1−β)1+β=16​(1−β)(1−β)​(1+β)2=16(1+β)2,\displaystyle=\frac{8}{1-\beta^{2}}\cdot\frac{2(1-\beta)}{1+\beta}=\frac{16(1-\beta)}{(1-\beta)(1+\beta)^{2}}=\frac{16}{(1+\beta)^{2}}, (66)
1ρ​∑t=1T−1α​𝕀refresh​Rt\displaystyle\frac{1}{\rho}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\alpha\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{refresh}}R_{t} =81−β2​∑t=1T−1α​𝕀refresh​Rt.\displaystyle=\frac{8}{1-\beta^{2}}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\alpha\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{refresh}}R_{t}. (67)

Substituting (64)–(67) into (63), we obtain

∑t=0T−1𝔼​‖Ut​mt​Vt⊤−∇f​(wt)‖2≤\displaystyle\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\left\|U_{t}m_{t}V_{t}^{\top}-\nabla f(w_{t})\right\|^{2}\leq\; 81−β2​𝔼​‖U0​m0​V0⊤−∇f​(w0)‖2\displaystyle\frac{8}{1-\beta^{2}}\,\mathbb{E}\left\|U_{0}m_{0}V_{0}^{\top}-\nabla f(w_{0})\right\|^{2} (68)
+81−β2∑t=1T−1α𝕀refreshRt\displaystyle+\frac{8}{1-\beta^{2}}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\alpha\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{refresh}}R_{t}
+8​(5−β2)​L2(1−β2)2∑t=1T−1𝔼∥wt−wt−1∥2\displaystyle+\frac{8(5-\beta^{2})L^{2}}{(1-\beta^{2})^{2}}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\|w_{t}-w_{t-1}\|^{2}
+16​(1−β)1+β∑t=1T−1σt2+16(1+β)2∑t=1T−1Δt.\displaystyle+\frac{16(1-\beta)}{1+\beta}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\sigma_{t}^{2}+\frac{16}{(1+\beta)^{2}}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\Delta_{t}.

We keep the refresh mismatch contribution ∑𝕀refresh​Rt\sum\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{refresh}}R_{t} for later discussion.

B.5 Part 5: Descent lemma and the final stationarity bound (keeping RtR_{t})

Assumption (smoothness).

Assume ff is LL-smooth, i.e., for all x,yx,y,

f⁡(y)≤f⁡(x)+⟨∇f​(x),y−x⟩+L2​‖y−x‖2.f(y)\leq f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{L}{2}\|y-x\|^{2}. (69)

Update rule.

Consider the update

wt+1=wt−η​m~t,wherem~t:=Ut​mt​Vt⊤.w_{t+1}=w_{t}-\eta\,\widetilde{m}_{t},\qquad\text{where}\qquad\widetilde{m}_{t}:=U_{t}m_{t}V_{t}^{\top}. (70)
Lemma 2 (Descent lemma for wt+1=wt−η​m~tw_{t+1}=w_{t}-\eta\widetilde{m}_{t}).

Under (69) and (70), for any t≥0t\geq 0,

f⁡(wt+1)≤\displaystyle f(w_{t+1})\leq\; f⁡(wt)−η2​‖∇f​(wt)‖2−(12​η−L2)​‖wt+1−wt‖2+η2​‖m~t−∇f​(wt)‖2.\displaystyle f(w_{t})-\frac{\eta}{2}\|\nabla f(w_{t})\|^{2}-\left(\frac{1}{2\eta}-\frac{L}{2}\right)\|w_{t+1}-w_{t}\|^{2}+\frac{\eta}{2}\|\widetilde{m}_{t}-\nabla f(w_{t})\|^{2}. (71)
Proof.

Apply LL-smoothness (69) with x=wtx=w_{t} and y=wt+1y=w_{t+1}:

f⁡(wt+1)\displaystyle f(w_{t+1}) ≤f⁡(wt)+⟨∇f​(wt),wt+1−wt⟩+L2​‖wt+1−wt‖2.\displaystyle\leq f(w_{t})+\langle\nabla f(w_{t}),w_{t+1}-w_{t}\rangle+\frac{L}{2}\|w_{t+1}-w_{t}\|^{2}. (72)

Using (70), we have wt+1−wt=−η​m~tw_{t+1}-w_{t}=-\eta\widetilde{m}_{t}, hence

⟨∇f​(wt),wt+1−wt⟩\displaystyle\langle\nabla f(w_{t}),w_{t+1}-w_{t}\rangle =−η⁡⟨∇f​(wt),m~t⟩=−η⁡⟨∇f​(wt),∇f​(wt)+(m~t−∇f​(wt))⟩\displaystyle=-\eta\langle\nabla f(w_{t}),\widetilde{m}_{t}\rangle=-\eta\left\langle\nabla f(w_{t}),\nabla f(w_{t})+(\widetilde{m}_{t}-\nabla f(w_{t}))\right\rangle
=−η​‖∇f​(wt)‖2−η⁡⟨∇f​(wt),m~t−∇f​(wt)⟩.\displaystyle=-\eta\|\nabla f(w_{t})\|^{2}-\eta\langle\nabla f(w_{t}),\widetilde{m}_{t}-\nabla f(w_{t})\rangle. (73)

Apply Young’s inequality −⟨a,b⟩≤12​‖a‖2+12​‖b‖2-\langle a,b\rangle\leq\frac{1}{2}\|a\|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\|b\|^{2} to the last term in (73) with a=∇f​(wt)a=\nabla f(w_{t}) and b=m~t−∇f​(wt)b=\widetilde{m}_{t}-\nabla f(w_{t}):

−η⁡⟨∇f​(wt),m~t−∇f​(wt)⟩≤η2​‖∇f​(wt)‖2+η2​‖m~t−∇f​(wt)‖2.-\eta\langle\nabla f(w_{t}),\widetilde{m}_{t}-\nabla f(w_{t})\rangle\leq\frac{\eta}{2}\|\nabla f(w_{t})\|^{2}+\frac{\eta}{2}\|\widetilde{m}_{t}-\nabla f(w_{t})\|^{2}. (74)

Combining (72)–(74) gives

f⁡(wt+1)\displaystyle f(w_{t+1}) ≤f⁡(wt)−η​‖∇f​(wt)‖2+η2​‖∇f​(wt)‖2+η2​‖m~t−∇f​(wt)‖2+L2​‖wt+1−wt‖2\displaystyle\leq f(w_{t})-\eta\|\nabla f(w_{t})\|^{2}+\frac{\eta}{2}\|\nabla f(w_{t})\|^{2}+\frac{\eta}{2}\|\widetilde{m}_{t}-\nabla f(w_{t})\|^{2}+\frac{L}{2}\|w_{t+1}-w_{t}\|^{2}
=f⁡(wt)−η2​‖∇f​(wt)‖2+η2​‖m~t−∇f​(wt)‖2+L2​‖wt+1−wt‖2.\displaystyle=f(w_{t})-\frac{\eta}{2}\|\nabla f(w_{t})\|^{2}+\frac{\eta}{2}\|\widetilde{m}_{t}-\nabla f(w_{t})\|^{2}+\frac{L}{2}\|w_{t+1}-w_{t}\|^{2}. (75)

Finally, rewrite L2​‖wt+1−wt‖2=−(12​η−L2)​‖wt+1−wt‖2+12​η​‖wt+1−wt‖2\frac{L}{2}\|w_{t+1}-w_{t}\|^{2}=-\left(\frac{1}{2\eta}-\frac{L}{2}\right)\|w_{t+1}-w_{t}\|^{2}+\frac{1}{2\eta}\|w_{t+1}-w_{t}\|^{2}, and note that 12​η​‖wt+1−wt‖2=η2​‖m~t‖2\frac{1}{2\eta}\|w_{t+1}-w_{t}\|^{2}=\frac{\eta}{2}\|\widetilde{m}_{t}\|^{2}. This yields (71). (Equivalently, one can directly expand ‖m~t‖2=‖∇f​(wt)+(m~t−∇f​(wt))‖2\|\widetilde{m}_{t}\|^{2}=\|\nabla f(w_{t})+(\widetilde{m}_{t}-\nabla f(w_{t}))\|^{2} and rearrange.) ∎

Summing Lemma 2.

Taking expectation in (71) and summing from t=0t=0 to T−1T-1 yields

η2​∑t=0T−1𝔼​‖∇f​(wt)‖2≤\displaystyle\frac{\eta}{2}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\|\nabla f(w_{t})\|^{2}\leq\; 𝔼⁡[f⁡(w0)−f⁡(wT)]+η2​∑t=0T−1𝔼​‖m~t−∇f​(wt)‖2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\big[f(w_{0})-f(w_{T})\big]+\frac{\eta}{2}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\|\widetilde{m}_{t}-\nabla f(w_{t})\|^{2} (76)
−(12​η−L2)∑t=0T−1𝔼∥wt+1−wt∥2.\displaystyle-\left(\frac{1}{2\eta}-\frac{L}{2}\right)\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\|w_{t+1}-w_{t}\|^{2}. (77)

Define Δ​f:=𝔼⁡[f⁡(w0)−f⋆]\Delta f:=\mathbb{E}[f(w_{0})-f^{\star}] (f⋆f^{\star} is a lower bound). Multiply both sides of (77) by 2η\frac{2}{\eta} to obtain

∑t=0T−1𝔼​‖∇f​(wt)‖2≤\displaystyle\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\|\nabla f(w_{t})\|^{2}\leq\; 2​Δ​fη+∑t=0T−1𝔼​‖m~t−∇f​(wt)‖2−(1η2−Lη)​∑t=0T−1𝔼​‖wt+1−wt‖2.\displaystyle\frac{2\Delta f}{\eta}+\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\|\widetilde{m}_{t}-\nabla f(w_{t})\|^{2}-\left(\frac{1}{\eta^{2}}-\frac{L}{\eta}\right)\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\|w_{t+1}-w_{t}\|^{2}. (78)

Substitute the bound from Part 4 (keeping ∑𝕀refresh​Rt\sum\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{refresh}}R_{t}).

From Part 4 (Eq. (68)), we have

∑t=0T−1𝔼​‖m~t−∇f​(wt)‖2≤\displaystyle\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\|\widetilde{m}_{t}-\nabla f(w_{t})\|^{2}\leq\; 81−β2​𝔼​‖m~0−∇f​(w0)‖2+81−β2​∑t=1T−1α​𝕀refresh​Rt\displaystyle\frac{8}{1-\beta^{2}}\,\mathbb{E}\|\widetilde{m}_{0}-\nabla f(w_{0})\|^{2}+\frac{8}{1-\beta^{2}}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\alpha\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{refresh}}R_{t}
+8​(5−β2)​L2(1−β2)2∑t=1T−1𝔼∥wt−wt−1∥2+16​(1−β)1+β∑t=1T−1σt2+16(1+β)2∑t=1T−1Δt.\displaystyle+\frac{8(5-\beta^{2})L^{2}}{(1-\beta^{2})^{2}}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\|w_{t}-w_{t-1}\|^{2}+\frac{16(1-\beta)}{1+\beta}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\sigma_{t}^{2}+\frac{16}{(1+\beta)^{2}}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\Delta_{t}. for some constants κU,κV≥0\kappa_{U},\kappa_{V}\geq 0.

Appendix C More about Experiments

C.1 Pre-Training Hyperparameters

We introduce details of the LLaMA architecture and hyperparameters used for pre-training. Table 5 shows the most hyperparameters of LLaMA models across model sizes.We use a max sequence length of 256 for all models,with a batch size of 262K tokens for LLaMA-60M and LLaMA-130M , and a batch size of 131K tokens for LLaMA-350M and LLaMA-1B. For all experiments,we adopt learning rate warmup for the first 10% of the training steps,and use cosine annealing for the learning rate schedule, decaying to 10% of the initial learning rate.For all model sizes, we use a learning rate of 0.01. For the LLaMA-60M model, we apply a scaling factor of 0.5, while the remaining models use a scaling factor of 0.75.

C.2 More experiment results

We present additional experimental results in Table 6.

C.3 Details of Fine-Tuning on GLUE

We fine-tune the pre-trained RoBERTa-Base model on the GLUE benchmark.We trained the model for 30 epochs with a batch size of 16 for all tasks except for CoLA, which uses a batch size of 32.We tune the learning rate and scale factor for TSR. Table 7 shows the hyperparameters used for fine-tuning RoBERTa-Base for TSR.
